questions.hint: Use SOH CAH TOA to set up an equation.
questions.solution: Relative to the \(71^\circ\) angle, the side of length \(12.6\text{ cm}\) is the adjacent side and \(h\text{ cm}\) (opposite the right angle) is the hypotenuse. Using \(\cos 71^\circ = \frac{12.6}{h}\), we get \(h = \frac{12.6}{\cos 71^\circ} \approx 38.70\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Identify the sides relative to the given angle \(\theta = 71^\circ\): the side opposite the \(90^\circ\) right-angle marker is the Hypotenuse (\(h\text{ cm}\)), and the side between \(71^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) is the Adjacent side (\(12.6\text{ cm}\)).

questions.stem: The point \(Y\) is on a bearing of \(065°\text{T}\) from point \(X\), and point \(Z\) is on a bearing of \(165°\text{T}\) from \(Y\). The size of \(\angle XYZ\) is:
questions.hint: The bearing from \(X\) to \(Y\) and the bearing from \(Y\) back to \(X\) differ by \(180°\). Use this to find the angle between \(YX\) and \(YZ\).

steps.explain: The bearing of \(X\) from \(Y\) (looking back) is the bearing of \(Y\) from \(X\) plus \(180°\).
The angle \(\angle XYZ\) is the difference between the bearing to \(X\) and the bearing to \(Z\), measured from \(Y\).

questions.stem: The diagonals of a trapezium \(ABCD\) make angles of \(30°\) as shown. The base \(CD\) has length \(10\) units. The perimeter of the trapezium is:
questions.hint: Let the diagonals intersect at a point — each of the four small triangles formed has a \(30°\) or related angle, and by symmetry several sides turn out equal.

steps.explain: Since the diagonal angles are both marked \(30°\) at \(D\) and \(C\), and \(AB \parallel DC\), the triangle formed by the diagonals and base has \(\angle BDC=30°\).
steps.work: \(\angle BOC=180°-30°-30°=120°\) (angle sum, where \(O\) is the intersection of the diagonals)

steps.explain: Using the trapezium's symmetry (both base angles at \(D\) and \(C\) equal \(30°\)) and the cosine ratio, each leg (\(AD\) and \(BC\)) and the top \(AB\) work out equal to \(5\) units, following the marked geometry of the diagram.
steps.work: \(AD = BC = AB = 5\) units (from the \(30°\)-\(30°\) isosceles construction)

steps.explain: Add all four sides to find the perimeter.

questions.stem: Daniel sailed due south for 40 km. Then he sailed due east for 30 km to reach a reef. What is the true bearing of the reef from Daniel's starting point?
questions.hint: Find the angle east of south using \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{30}{40}\), then convert to a true bearing (measured clockwise from North).

steps.explain: Find the angle between the southward leg and the direct line to the reef, using the right triangle formed (40 km south, 30 km east).
Convert this to a true bearing: due South is \(180°\text{T}\), and the reef is \(36.87°\) toward East (i.e. back toward \(90°\)), so subtract from \(180°\).
Round to the nearest whole degree.

questions.stem: In the right-angled triangle, find the value of \(y\) correct to 2 decimal places, where the angle is \(61°\), and the opposite side is \(5\) cm.
questions.hint: Use the sine ratio: sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse

steps.explain: We have a right triangle with an angle of 61°, and the opposite side is 5 cm. We need to find the hypotenuse y.
steps.work:
<svg viewBox="0 0 280 260" width="100%" height="auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc;border-radius:12px;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;max-width:280px;display:block;margin:0 auto;">
  <polygon points="60,220 220,220 60,60" fill="#dbeafe" opacity="0.5" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/>

  <text x="75" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" stroke="#f8fafc" stroke-width="4" stroke-linejoin="round">61°</text><text x="75" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#b45309">61°</text>
  <text x="140" y="244" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" stroke="#f8fafc" stroke-width="4" stroke-linejoin="round">5 cm</text><text x="140" y="244" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1d4ed8">5 cm</text>

\(\sin(61°) = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{5}{y}\)

steps.explain: Rearrange to solve for y by dividing 5 by sin(61°).

questions.stem: In the right-angled triangle, find the value of \(x\) correct to 2 decimal places, where the angle is 31 degrees 48 minutes and the opposite side is \(20\) cm.
questions.hint: Use the tangent ratio: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent

steps.explain: We have a right triangle with a 90° angle at the top vertex. The angle 31°48' is at the bottom-left, the adjacent side is 20, and x is the side opposite this angle.
steps.work:
<svg viewBox="0 0 320 260" width="100%" height="auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc;border-radius:12px;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;max-width:280px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><polygon points="150,60 55,215 270,205" fill="#dbeafe" opacity="0.5" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="142.86,72.03999999999999 152.8,81.83999999999999 159.94,69.8" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="78.5" y="137.5" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" stroke="#f8fafc" stroke-width="4" stroke-linejoin="round">20</text><text x="78.5" y="137.5" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1d4ed8">20</text><text x="230" y="132.5" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" stroke="#f8fafc" stroke-width="4" stroke-linejoin="round">x</text><text x="230" y="132.5" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">x</text><text x="79" y="205" text-anchor="start" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" stroke="#f8fafc" stroke-width="4" stroke-linejoin="round">31°48'</text><text x="79" y="205" text-anchor="start" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#b45309">31°48'</text></svg>

questions.stem: In the right-angled triangle, find \(θ\) correct to the nearest degree, where the adjacent side is \(19\) cm and the hypotenuse is \(26\) cm.
questions.hint: Use the inverse cosine function: θ = cos⁻¹(adjacent/hypotenuse)

questions.stem:
Find \(h\), correct to the nearest centimetre.

<svg viewBox="0 0 360 200" width="100%" height="auto" style="max-width: 440px; display: block; margin: 1rem auto; background-color: #f8fafc; border-radius: 16px; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; padding: 1rem;" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="40" y1="160" x2="280" y2="160" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="240" y1="160" x2="240" y2="40" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="40" y1="160" x2="240" y2="40" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="160" y1="160" x2="240" y2="40" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2" /><polyline points="225,160 225,145 240,145" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="30" y="180" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">P</text><text x="150" y="180" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Q</text><text x="245" y="180" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">R</text><text x="245" y="35" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">S</text><text x="100" y="190" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#3b82f6" font-weight="600">10 m</text><text x="255" y="100" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#ef4444" font-weight="600" font-style="italic">h</text><path d="M 80 160 A 40 40 0 0 0 62 146" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="85" y="155" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">30°</text><path d="M 180 160 A 20 20 0 0 0 172 142" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="185" y="150" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">72°</text></svg>
questions.hint: Set up equations for \(h\) using the two right-angled triangles \(\triangle SPR\) and \(\triangle SQR\). Convert the final answer to centimetres.

steps.explain: Looking at the diagram, we have two right-angled triangles sharing the same height \(h\): \(\triangle PRS\) (the larger one) and \(\triangle QRS\) (the smaller one). Let's express \(PR\) and \(QR\) in terms of \(h\).
From the graph, the distance \(PQ\) is the difference between \(PR\) and \(QR\). Set up an equation using \(PQ = 10\).
Factor out \(h\) and solve for it in metres.
The question asks for the height correct to the nearest centimetre. Convert \(h\) to cm.

questions.stem: (c) A boat starts at port \(A\) and travels on a bearing of \(222°\text{T}\) until it reaches point \(B\). From \(B\), two buoys \(X\) and \(Y\) are seen due South of \(B\); \(Y\) is known to be 200 m due South of \(X\). The boat continues on the same course (\(222°\text{T}\)) until it reaches point \(C\). From \(C\), the bearing of \(X\) is \(140°\text{T}\) and the bearing of \(Y\) is \(165°\text{T}\). Draw a diagram showing all of the information given above.

steps.explain: Mark the North direction at \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). Draw the boat's path \(A\to B\to C\) as a single straight line on a bearing of \(222°\text{T}\) (since it continues on the same course).
steps.work: Draw \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) collinear, with bearing \(222°\text{T}\) marked at \(A\) (and equivalently at \(B\)).

steps.explain: From \(B\), draw a line due South showing \(X\) then \(Y\) (200 m further south of \(X\)) on this line.
steps.work: Mark \(X\) and \(Y\) on a vertical line south of \(B\), with \(XY=200\) m.

steps.explain: From \(C\), draw lines to \(X\) and \(Y\) at the given bearings \(140°\text{T}\) and \(165°\text{T}\) respectively.
steps.work: Draw \(CX\) at bearing \(140°\text{T}\) and \(CY\) at bearing \(165°\text{T}\) from \(C\), as shown in the completed diagram above.

questions.stem: A plane flies from Melbourne at a bearing of \(310°\). After flying \(600\) km, it reaches point P. How far north of Melbourne is the plane when it reaches Point P (to the nearest km)?
questions.hint: Convert bearing to angle from north, then use cosine to find the northward component.

steps.explain: Bearing 310° is measured clockwise from north. Since 310° is more than 270° (west) but less than 360° (north again), it's in the NW quadrant. The angle between north and the bearing 310° ray is 360° − 310° = 50°, so this is equivalent to N50°W.

questions.stem: A man standing on a vertical cliff \(52\) metres high notices a shark in the water. If the angle of depression is 41 degrees 17 minutes, how far is the shark from the base of the cliff (to the nearest metre)?
questions.hint: Angle of depression = angle at water level (alternate interior angles). Use tan(θ) = height/distance.

steps.explain: The cliff is vertical (52 m), the water surface is horizontal, and there's a right angle where they meet at the base. The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the shark's position (alternate angles on the dashed horizontal line), so we can work with 41°17' at the shark's position.

questions.hint: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\) — but the adjacent side isn't given, so find it first with Pythagoras.

questions.hint: The 25° angle is measured clockwise from east to the route from A to B. First find that bearing from north, then reverse it to get the bearing of A from B.

steps.explain: At A, the north line is the starting direction for a bearing. East is 090°. The diagram gives a further 25° clockwise from east to line AB, so add these two angles to find the bearing from A to B.

steps.explain: The question asks for A from B, so reverse the direction along the same line AB. Reverse bearings differ by 180°; add 180° to the bearing just found.

keyPoints.note: East is 090°. Add the 25° at A to get A→B, then add 180° to reverse the direction.

questions.stem: A surveyor stands at a point A, which is due south of a tower T of height h m. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from A is 45°. The surveyor then walks 100 m due east to point B, from where the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 30°. Express the length of TB in terms of h.
questions.hint: In right triangle \(TOB\), \(OT=h\) is opposite \(30^\circ\), and \(TB\) is the hypotenuse. Use sine to relate these sides.

steps.explain: Focus on the right triangle formed by the tower, the ground, and the line of sight from B. Relative to the \(30^\circ\) angle at \(B\), \(OT=h\) is the opposite side and \(TB\) is the hypotenuse. The \(45^\circ\) angle at A and the \(100\text{ m}\) walk are not needed to find \(TB\).

steps.explain: Use the sine ratio because it connects the opposite side \(OT\) to the hypotenuse \(TB\). Substitute the known height and the angle of elevation.

steps.explain: Rearrange to make \(TB\) the subject, then use \(\sin 30^\circ=\frac12\). This confirms the required line of sight is twice the tower height.

keyPoints.note: In right triangle \(TOB\), \(OT=h\) is opposite the \(30^\circ\) angle at \(B\), and \(TB\) is the hypotenuse. Use the sine ratio.

questions.stem: A surveyor stands at a point A, which is due south of a tower OT of height \(h\text{ m}\). The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from A is \(45^\circ\). The surveyor then walks \(100\text{ m}\) due east to point B, from where she measures the angle of elevation of the top of the tower to be \(30^\circ\). Show that \(h=50\sqrt{2}\).
questions.hint: Start with the right triangle at A: use \(\tan45^\circ\) to relate the tower height \(OT=h\) to the ground distance \(OA\). Then find \(OB\) using the \(30^\circ\) elevation at B and apply Pythagoras in ground triangle \(AOB\).

steps.explain: Use the right triangle in the vertical plane through A, O, and T. At A, the angle is \(45^\circ\); the opposite side is the tower height \(OT=h\), and the adjacent side is the ground distance \(OA\). Apply tangent to find \(OA\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="360" height="210" viewBox="0 0 360 210"><path d="M70 165V45M70 165H190M70 45L190 165" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M70 151H84V165" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.3"/><path d="M170 165 A28 28 0 0 1 170.2 145.2" fill="none" stroke="#f97316" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M70 45V165" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M70 165H190" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="3"/><text x="54" y="40" font-size="12" fill="#334155">T</text><text x="53" y="183" font-size="12" fill="#334155">O</text><text x="194" y="183" font-size="12" fill="#334155">A</text><text x="31" y="108" font-size="12" fill="#1d4ed8">OT = h</text><text x="111" y="187" font-size="12" fill="#6d28d9">OA</text><text x="143" y="153" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">45°</text></svg>

steps.explain: In the vertical right triangle \(TOB\), the \(30^\circ\) angle at B has opposite side \(OT=h\) and adjacent side \(OB\). Use tangent to obtain the horizontal ground distance \(OB\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="360" height="210" viewBox="0 0 360 210"><path d="M70 165V45M70 165H275M70 45L275 165" fill="none" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M70 151H84V165" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.3"/><path d="M244 165 A31 31 0 0 1 249 149" fill="none" stroke="#f97316" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M70 45V165" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M70 165H275" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="3"/><text x="54" y="40" font-size="12" fill="#334155">T</text><text x="53" y="183" font-size="12" fill="#334155">O</text><text x="280" y="183" font-size="12" fill="#334155">B</text><text x="31" y="108" font-size="12" fill="#1d4ed8">OT = h</text><text x="155" y="187" font-size="12" fill="#6d28d9">OB</text><text x="220" y="153" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">30°</text></svg>

steps.explain: Now use the ground-plane right triangle \(AOB\). Since the walk is due east and \(OA\) is due south, \(\angle OAB=90^\circ\). Its legs are \(OA=h\) and \(AB=100\text{ m}\), while the hypotenuse is \(OB=h\sqrt3\). Substitute these side lengths into Pythagoras, then take the positive root because a height is positive.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="360" height="210" viewBox="0 0 360 210"><path d="M70 160V45M70 160H270M70 45L270 160" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M70 145H85V160" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.3"/><path d="M70 160V45" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M70 160H270" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M70 45L270 160" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="3"/><text x="53" y="40" font-size="12" fill="#334155">O</text><text x="52" y="178" font-size="12" fill="#334155">A</text><text x="275" y="178" font-size="12" fill="#334155">B</text><text x="32" y="105" font-size="12" fill="#1d4ed8">OA = h</text><text x="146" y="184" font-size="12" fill="#6d28d9">AB = 100 m</text><text x="163" y="76" font-size="12" fill="#15803d">OB = h√3</text></svg>

keyPoints.text: The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from A is \(45^\circ\).
keyPoints.note: In right triangle \(AOT\), \(OT=h\) is opposite \(45^\circ\) and \(OA\) is adjacent, so \(\tan45^\circ=OT/OA\).

questions.stem: A surveyor stands at a point A, which is due south of a tower OT of height \(h\text{ m}\). The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from A is \(45^\circ\). The surveyor then walks \(100\text{ m}\) due east to point B, from where she measures the angle of elevation of the top of the tower to be \(30^\circ\). Calculate the bearing of B from the base of the tower.
questions.hint: First use the elevation angles to determine the southward ground distance \(OA\). In the ground view, \(AB=100\text{ m}\) is due east; use the right triangle to find the angle from south, then convert it to a bearing measured clockwise from north.

steps.explain: In the vertical right triangle \(AOT\), the angle at \(A\) is \(45^\circ\). The opposite side is the tower height \(OT=h\), and the adjacent side is the southward ground distance \(OA\). Use tangent to relate them.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="360" height="210" viewBox="0 0 360 210"><path d="M70 165V45M70 165H190M70 45L190 165" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M70 151H84V165" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.3"/><path d="M170 165 A28 28 0 0 1 170 145" fill="none" stroke="#f97316" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M70 45V165" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M70 165H190" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="3"/><text x="54" y="40" font-size="12" fill="#334155">T</text><text x="53" y="183" font-size="12" fill="#334155">O</text><text x="194" y="183" font-size="12" fill="#334155">A</text><text x="31" y="108" font-size="12" fill="#1d4ed8">OT = h</text><text x="111" y="187" font-size="12" fill="#6d28d9">OA</text><text x="143" y="153" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">45°</text></svg>

steps.explain: Use the elevation at \(B\) in the vertical right triangle \(TOB\). Relative to \(30^\circ\), \(OT=h\) is opposite and \(OB\) is adjacent. Then use the ground right triangle \(AOB\): \(AB=100\text{ m}\), \(OA=h\), and \(OB\) is its hypotenuse. This determines \(h\), and therefore \(OA\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="360" height="210" viewBox="0 0 360 210"><path d="M70 160V45M70 160H265M70 45L265 160" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M70 145H85V160" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.3"/><path d="M70 160V45" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M70 160H265" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M70 45L265 160" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="3"/><text x="53" y="40" font-size="12" fill="#334155">O</text><text x="52" y="178" font-size="12" fill="#334155">A</text><text x="270" y="178" font-size="12" fill="#334155">B</text><text x="30" y="105" font-size="12" fill="#1d4ed8">OA = h</text><text x="127" y="184" font-size="12" fill="#6d28d9">AB = 100 m</text><text x="144" y="72" font-size="12" fill="#15803d">OB = h√3</text></svg>

steps.explain: In the ground-plane triangle, \(OA=50\sqrt2\text{ m}\) is due south and \(AB=100\text{ m}\) is due east. Let \(\alpha\) be the angle east of south at \(O\). Relative to \(\alpha\), \(AB\) is opposite and \(OA\) is adjacent. Calculate \(\alpha\) with tangent.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="360" height="220" viewBox="0 0 360 220"><path d="M75 50V165M75 165H260M75 50L260 165" fill="none" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M75 50V165" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M75 165H260" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M75 50L260 165" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M75 150H90V165" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.3"/><path d="M75 20V50" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M75 83 A33 33 0 0 0 103 67" fill="none" stroke="#f97316" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="61" y="45" font-size="12" fill="#334155">O</text><text x="58" y="183" font-size="12" fill="#334155">A</text><text x="265" y="180" font-size="12" fill="#334155">B</text><text x="84" y="112" font-size="11" fill="#1d4ed8">OA = 50√2</text><text x="139" y="188" font-size="12" fill="#6d28d9">AB = 100</text><text x="158" y="78" font-size="12" fill="#15803d">OB</text><text x="87" y="75" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">α</text><text x="64" y="15" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">N</text></svg>

steps.explain: A bearing is measured clockwise from north. The south direction is \(180^\circ\), and \(\alpha\) is measured east from south, so subtract \(\alpha\) from \(180^\circ\). State the bearing using three figures.

keyPoints.note: A bearing is measured clockwise from north. Here the ground direction to B is southeast; first find the angle east of south, then subtract it from \(180^\circ\).

questions.stem: The sun casts a shadow from a tree. Find the length of the shadow, to the nearest cm, if the height of the tree is 3.2 m and the angle of elevation of the sun is 78°.

meta.source: Sydney Girls High School Year 10 Yearly Examination 2011

questions.hint: The tree height is opposite the 78° angle; the shadow is adjacent. Use tangent, then convert metres to centimetres.

keyPoints.text: height of the tree is 3.2 m
keyPoints.note: This is the side opposite the angle of elevation.

keyPoints.text: angle of elevation of the sun is 78°
keyPoints.note: The ground shadow is adjacent to this angle, so tangent connects the two lengths.

steps.explain: The tree, ground, and sun ray form a right triangle. Relative to the 78° angle, the tree height is opposite and the shadow length (s) is adjacent.

questions.stem: The figure above shows the side view of a bridge opened to let boats pass underneath. When the equal arms of the bridge PA and QB are lowered, they meet exactly to form the straight roadway PQ, which is 50 m long. When the arms PA and QB are raised through an angle \(\theta\) as shown, the “corridor” AB is 12 m wide. Calculate the size of angle \(\theta\), to the nearest degree.

meta.source: Sydney Girls High School Year 10 Yearly Examination 2011

questions.hint: The raised arms are each 25 m. The 50 m roadway exceeds the 12 m corridor by 38 m; split that difference equally at the two ends, then use cosine in one right triangle.

keyPoints.note: This is the full lowered roadway length.
Subtract this width from 50 m; the leftover width is shared equally by the two sides.

keyPoints.text: equal arms of the bridge PA and QB
keyPoints.note: Each sloping side has length 25 m as shown; use it as the hypotenuse.

steps.explain: The two equal bridge arms are each 25 m long. The difference between the lowered roadway and the corridor is split equally between left and right.
steps.work: \(50-12=38\text{ m},\qquad\text{horizontal offset on each side}=\frac{38}{2}=19\text{ m}\)

steps.explain: Opposite and adjacent: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}\).
Make \(h\) the subject and use the exact value \(\tan 30^{\circ}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).
Check: \(2\sqrt{3}\approx 3.46\) and \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3.46}=30^{\circ}\) ✓. Option B comes from \(\tan 30^{\circ}=\dfrac{h}{2}\) (opposite and adjacent swapped).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: The 30 degree angle is at the apex: radius is opposite, height is adjacent, use tan.

Check with the angles measured from the EAST horizontal line at \(B\): \(BC\) (bearing \(060^{\circ}\)) is \(90^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=30^{\circ}\) ABOVE it, and \(BP\) (bearing \(125^{\circ}\)) is \(125^{\circ}-90^{\circ}=35^{\circ}\) BELOW it, so \(\angle PBC=30^{\circ}+35^{\circ}=65^{\circ}\) ✓.
Option D (125°) is just the back-bearing, option C only the angle above the west line.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Back-bearing is the bearing plus or minus 180; the angle between two bearings is their difference.

questions.hint: Find \(\theta\) first. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. The opposite side is across from \(\theta\). The adjacent side is the one left over that touches \(\theta\).

steps.explain: Locate \(\theta\): it is the angle at the bottom-left corner. The right angle is at the bottom-right corner.
The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle: the sloping side (purple).
The opposite side is the side directly across from \(\theta\): the vertical side (red).
The adjacent side is the remaining side that touches \(\theta\) (and is not the hypotenuse): the horizontal bottom side (green). Label it \(x\).

questions.stem: Find the exact value of \(x\). The right-angled triangle has legs \(5\ \text{cm}\) and \(7\ \text{cm}\) and hypotenuse \(x\ \text{cm}\).

questions.hint: Use Pythagoras: hypotenuse\(^2\) = sum of the squares of the other two sides. \"Exact\" means leave the answer as a surd (do not use a calculator decimal).

steps.explain: Identify the hypotenuse: the side opposite the right angle is \(x\) (purple). The legs are 5 (red) and 7 (green).

steps.explain: Write Pythagoras' theorem.
Square and add.
Square root (positive, since a length). Leave it exact.
Why not the others: \(\sqrt{24}\) subtracts the squares (use that only to find a leg); 12 adds the sides; \(\sqrt{35}\) uses \(5\times7\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Exact value = surd, not a rounded decimal.

questions.stem: Evaluate \(\sin 72^{\circ}\), correct to three decimal places.
questions.hint: Set the calculator to DEGREE mode, then press sin 72 and round to 3 decimal places (look at the 4th decimal place).

steps.explain: Check the calculator is in degree mode (D or DEG), because the angle is in degrees.
Calculate.
Round to 3 decimal places: the 4th decimal digit is 0, so round down.
Why not the others: \(0.309\) is \(\cos72^{\circ}\); \(3.078\) is \(\tan72^{\circ}\); \(0.254\) is what you get in RADIAN mode.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Calculator must be in degree mode.

questions.stem: Convert \(43.2^{\circ}\) into degrees and minutes.
questions.hint: \(1^{\circ}=60'\). Keep the whole 43 degrees, then multiply the decimal part by 60 to get minutes.

steps.explain: Whole degrees: \(43^{\circ}\). Decimal part: \(0.2^{\circ}\).
Convert the decimal part to minutes: there are 60 minutes in 1 degree.
Put them together.

Check with the calculator DMS key: \(43.2\to43^{\circ}12'0''\) ✓. Why not the others: \(43^{\circ}20'\) treats 0.2 as 20 minutes; \(43^{\circ}2'\) treats it as 2 minutes; \(43^{\circ}48'\) uses \(0.8\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Decimal degrees times 60 gives minutes.

questions.stem: Solve the following equation. \(\cos 54^{\circ}=\dfrac{x}{5}\)  (Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.hint: Multiply both sides by 5 to get \(x\) alone, then use the calculator in degree mode.

steps.explain: The unknown \(x\) is divided by 5. Undo this by multiplying both sides by 5.
Calculate: \(\cos54^{\circ}=0.58778\ldots\).
Round to 2 decimal places (3rd decimal digit is 8, round up).
Why not the others: \(4.05=5\sin54^{\circ}\); \(8.51=5\div\cos54^{\circ}\) (dividing instead of multiplying); \(6.88=5\tan54^{\circ}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Multiply both sides by the denominator first.

questions.stem: Find the unknown angle \(\theta\), correct to the nearest minute. The right-angled triangle has hypotenuse \(7.3\), base \(4\) (touching \(\theta\)), and \(\theta\) is at the bottom-right corner.

questions.hint: From \(\theta\): the side 4 touches \(\theta\) (adjacent) and 7.3 is the hypotenuse. Adjacent and hypotenuse: cosine. Use \(\cos^{-1}\), then convert the decimal to minutes.

steps.explain: Label from \(\theta\): adjacent = 4 (green), hypotenuse = 7.3 (purple).

steps.explain: Adjacent and hypotenuse: use cosine.
Use the inverse function \(\cos^{-1}\).
Convert to degrees and minutes: \(0.7738^{\circ}\times60=46.4'\), nearest minute \(46'\).

Why not the others: using \(\sin^{-1}\) gives the OTHER angle \(33^{\circ}14'\); \(61^{\circ}17'=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7.3}{4}\right)\) and \(28^{\circ}43'=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{7.3}\right)\) use the wrong ratio.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Adjacent + hypotenuse = cos; use cos inverse.

steps.explain: Draw the tower as a vertical line of height 78 m, and the ground as a horizontal line. The cliff edge is on the ground.

questions.stem: The angle of depression from the top of a 78 m tall tower to the edge of a cliff in the same plane is \(12^{\circ}\). Hence, or otherwise, calculate how far is the edge of the cliff from the base of the tower, correct to one decimal place.
questions.hint: The angle of elevation from the cliff edge to the tower top is also \(12^{\circ}\) (alternate angles). In the right-angled triangle, 78 is OPPOSITE that angle and the distance is ADJACENT.

steps.explain: Alternate angles: the horizontal at the top of the tower is parallel to the ground, so the angle at the cliff edge inside the triangle is also \(12^{\circ}\). 78 m is opposite it; the unknown distance \(d\) is adjacent.

steps.explain: Opposite and adjacent: tangent.
\(d\) is in the denominator: \(d=\dfrac{78}{\tan12^{\circ}}\).
Calculate and round to 1 decimal place.
Why not the others: \(16.6=78\tan12^{\circ}\) (multiplied); \(375.2=78\div\sin12^{\circ}\) (that is the line of sight); \(76.3=78\cos12^{\circ}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

Check with the rule: reverse bearing \(=323^{\circ}-180^{\circ}\).
Why not the others: \(037^{\circ}\) is the angle \(\theta\) itself; \(217^{\circ}=37^{\circ}+180^{\circ}\) (adds 180° to the wrong angle); \(323^{\circ}\) is the original bearing (Burke from Nyngan).
So the correct choice is option A.

meta.source: Killara High School 2023 Year 10 Mathematics Task 4A

questions.stem: Singha, \(S\), is 1200 metres from his home, \(H\), when he first sees an airplane. The angle of elevation from Singha to the plane at \(P\) is \(64^{\circ}\). Five minutes later the plane is directly above Singha's home at \(D\). The angle of elevation from Singha to \(D\) is \(23^{\circ}\). How far did the airplane travel from \(P\) to \(D\), to the nearest metre?

steps.explain: Drop a vertical from \(P\) to \(Q\) on \(HS\). Triangle \(SQP\): \(QP=HD=509.4\) is opposite \(64^{\circ}\), \(SQ\) is adjacent.
Solve for \(SQ\) (unknown in the denominator, so divide).
\(PD=HQ=HS-SQ\).

questions.stem: If \(x\) is acute, and \(\cos(2x-10)=\sin(x+40)\), find \(x\).
questions.hint: Sine and cosine of COMPLEMENTARY angles are equal: \(\sin A=\cos(90^{\circ}-A)\). Rewrite the sine as a cosine, then equate the angles.

steps.explain: Rewrite \(\sin(x+40)\) as a cosine using \(\sin A=\cos(90^{\circ}-A)\).
Equation becomes \(\cos(2x-10)=\cos(50-x)\). For acute angles equal cosines mean equal angles.
Solve: add \(x\) to both sides, then add 10.

Check: \(\cos(2\times20-10)=\cos30^{\circ}=0.866\) and \(\sin(20+40)=\sin60^{\circ}=0.866\) ✓. Why not the others: 30, 40, 25 do not make the two sides equal (e.g. \(x=30\): \(\cos50^{\circ}\ne\sin70^{\circ}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: sin A = cos(90° − A) for complementary angles.

questions.hint: Use the right triangle with angle 75°, opposite side BD = 2 + √3 and adjacent side AB = 1.

keyPoints.note: Keep the exact value; do not round the surd to a decimal.

steps.explain: From the diagram, BD = BC + CD and BC = √3.

questions.hint: Which two sides are involved? The 12 m side is ADJACENT to the 30° angle and \(x\) is the HYPOTENUSE — so use cosine: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}\). Use the exact value \(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

steps.explain: Label the sides from the 30° angle: 12 m is next to the angle (adjacent, blue) and \(x\) is opposite the right angle (hypotenuse, red).

Use the exact value \(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and solve for \(x\) (swap \(x\) and \(\cos 30^\circ\)).

Divide 24 by 3.

Rationalise at the end.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of the following, showing all working and giving answers in simplest form. You do not have to rationalise denominators. \(\cos 60^\circ \times \sin 45^\circ\)
questions.hint: Use the exact-value triangles: \(\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Then multiply the fractions.

steps.explain: Recall the exact values from the special triangles (30-60-90 and 45-45-90).
Substitute.
Multiply the numerators and the denominators.
(Rationalised: \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\) — an equivalent value; the question does not require it.)

keyPoints.note: Use special-triangle values.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of the following, showing all working and giving answers in simplest form. You do not have to rationalise denominators. \(\dfrac{\tan 30^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ}\)
questions.hint: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Dividing by a fraction = MULTIPLYING by its reciprocal.

steps.explain: Recall the exact values.
Substitute into the fraction.
Change the division into multiplication by the RECIPROCAL (flip the second fraction).
Multiply.

keyPoints.note: Use the exact values from the 30-60-90 triangle.

questions.hint: DC is opposite AB in rectangle ABCD, so DC = AB. Find AB using right triangle ABE (right-angled at E, since BE is vertical and AE is horizontal).
questions.solution: In right triangle ABE (right-angled at E): \(AB = \sqrt{AE^2+BE^2} = \sqrt{24^2+41^2} = \sqrt{2257}\). Since DC and AB are opposite sides of rectangle ABCD, \(DC = AB = \sqrt{2257}\).

questions.solution: In the vertical triangle (right-angled at the tree's base): \(\tan(32^\circ) = \frac{h}{50}\), so \(h = 50\tan(32^\circ) \approx 31.2\) m.

questions.solution: On the ground, triangle PQT is right-angled at P: \(QT = \sqrt{PQ^2+PT^2} = \sqrt{100^2+50^2} = \sqrt{12500} \approx 111.8\) m.

Take the square root and round to one decimal place.

questions.stem:
The base of a tree is situated \(50\) metres due north of a point \(P\). The angle of elevation of the top of the tree from \(P\) is \(32^\circ\). \(Q\) is a point \(100\) metres due east of \(P\).

Find the bearing of the tree from \(Q\), correct to one decimal place.
questions.hint: From Q, the tree lies north and west — first find the acute angle θ between north and QT using the right triangle PQT (right-angled at P), then convert to a true bearing.
questions.solution: From Q, the tree is in the north-west direction. θ (measured west of north) satisfies \(\tan\theta = \frac{PQ}{PT} = \frac{100}{50} = 2\), so \(\theta \approx 63.43^\circ\), giving a true bearing of \(360^\circ - 63.43^\circ \approx 296.6^\circ\).

steps.explain: From Q, the tree (T) lies to the north and west, since T is north of P and Q is east of P. Let θ be the acute angle at Q, measured from due north (from Q) around to the line QT — this is the angle in right triangle PQT at vertex Q, since QP points due west from Q.

In right triangle PQT (right-angled at P), θ is the angle at Q. Relative to θ, PT (the north-south leg) is opposite and PQ (the east-west leg) is adjacent — since θ is measured from the north-south direction.
Substitute the known distances and evaluate.
Since the tree is to the west of north from Q, the true bearing is measured clockwise from north, all the way around: \(360^\circ - \theta\). Round to one decimal place.

questions.stem:
Dillon and Eugene are both looking at a tower of height \(35\) metres. Dillon is standing due south of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be \(15^\circ\). Eugene is standing due east of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be \(20^\circ\).

Find, correct to one decimal place, the distance Dillon is from the foot of the tower.
questions.hint: In the vertical right triangle (right-angled at the tower's base), the tower height (35 m) is opposite Dillon's 15° angle of elevation, and Dillon's distance d is adjacent. Use the tangent ratio.
questions.solution: In the vertical triangle: \(\tan(15^\circ) = \frac{35}{d} \implies d = \frac{35}{\tan(15^\circ)} \approx 130.6\) m.

steps.explain: Dillon, the tower's base, and the tower's top form a right triangle, right-angled at the base. The height (35 m) is opposite Dillon's angle of elevation (15°), and Dillon's unknown distance d is adjacent.
Use the tangent ratio, since we know the opposite side and want the adjacent side.
Rearrange to make d the subject.
Evaluate the division and round to one decimal place.

questions.solution: In the vertical triangle: \(\tan(20^\circ) = \frac{35}{d} \implies d = \frac{35}{\tan(20^\circ)} \approx 96.2\) m.

steps.explain: Eugene, the tower's base, and the tower's top form a right triangle, right-angled at the base. The height (35 m) is opposite Eugene's angle of elevation (20°), and Eugene's unknown distance d is adjacent.

questions.stem:
Dillon and Eugene are both looking at a tower of height \(35\) metres. Dillon is standing due south of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be \(15^\circ\). Eugene is standing due east of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be \(20^\circ\).

Find, correct to one decimal place, the distance between Dillon and Eugene.
questions.hint: On the ground (plan view), Dillon, Eugene and the tower's base form a right triangle with the right angle at the tower's base (due south and due east are perpendicular directions). Use the distances found in the previous two parts.
questions.solution: On the ground, triangle (Dillon, tower base, Eugene) is right-angled at the tower's base: \(DE = \sqrt{130.6^2+96.2^2} \approx 162.2\) m.

steps.explain: On the ground, Dillon (due south of the tower) and Eugene (due east of the tower) form a right angle at the tower's base — south and east are perpendicular directions. Use the distances already found for Dillon and Eugene.
Apply Pythagoras' theorem, using the two distances-to-base as the legs of the right triangle.
Evaluate each square and add.
Take the square root and round to one decimal place.

questions.stem:
Dillon and Eugene are both looking at a tower of height \(35\) metres. Dillon is standing due south of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be \(15^\circ\). Eugene is standing due east of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be \(20^\circ\).

Find, correct to one decimal place, the bearing of Dillon from Eugene.
questions.hint: From Eugene, Dillon lies south and west — first find the acute angle φ between south and the line from Eugene to Dillon, using the right triangle (tower base, Dillon, Eugene), then convert to a true bearing.
questions.solution: From Eugene, Dillon is in the south-west direction. In the right triangle at the tower's base, \(\tan\varphi = \frac{96.2}{130.6} \approx 0.7366\), so \(\varphi \approx 36.4^\circ\) (west of south), giving a true bearing of \(180^\circ + 36.4^\circ \approx 216.4^\circ\).

steps.explain: From Eugene, Dillon lies to the south and west (Dillon is south of the tower, Eugene is east of the tower). Let φ be the acute angle at Eugene, between due south and the line to Dillon, inside the right triangle (tower base, Dillon, Eugene).
Relative to φ (measured from the south direction), the east-west offset (Eugene–base) is opposite and the north-south offset (Dillon–base) is adjacent.
Evaluate the ratio and apply the inverse tangent function.
Since Dillon is south-west of Eugene, the true bearing is measured clockwise from north, past east and south: \(180^\circ + \varphi\). Round to one decimal place.

questions.stem: From a point \(A\), a lighthouse is on a bearing of \(026^\circ\mathrm{T}\) and the top of the lighthouse is at angle of elevation of \(20.25^\circ\). From a point \(B\), the lighthouse is on a bearing of \(296^\circ\mathrm{T}\) and the top of the lighthouse is at angle of elevation of \(10.20^\circ\). If \(A\) and \(B\) are \(500\) metres apart, find the height of the lighthouse, correct to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: Bearings are absolute compass directions, so the angle at L between LA and LB equals the difference between the reverse bearings L→A and L→B — this gives a right angle here. Then use AL²+BL²=AB² together with the two elevation ratios (both equal to the height h) to solve for h.
questions.solution: Reverse bearings give ∠ALB = 90°. Solving AL·tan(20.25°)=BL·tan(10.20°) together with AL²+BL²=500² gives AL≈219.2 m, BL≈449.4 m, so h = AL·tan(20.25°) ≈ 81 m.

steps.explain: The bearing of L from A is 026°T, so the reverse bearing (of A from L) is 026°+180°=206°. The bearing of L from B is 296°T, so the reverse bearing (of B from L) is 296°−180°=116°. Since bearings are absolute compass directions, the angle at L between LA and LB is the difference between these reverse bearings.

In the vertical planes through A and B, the lighthouse height h is opposite each elevation angle, with AL and BL as the adjacent (horizontal) legs. Since triangle ALB is right-angled at L (from the plan view), also AL²+BL²=AB².
Substitute AL = BL·\(\frac{\tan(10.20^\circ)}{\tan(20.25^\circ)}\) ≈ 0.4877·BL into the Pythagorean equation and solve for BL, then AL.
Substitute AL back into the height equation and round to the nearest metre.

A vertical cliff runs north-south. An observer at the top \(T\) of the cliff, directly above the point \(F\) at sea level, sees a yacht at \(A\), \(200\) m due east of \(F\). The angle of depression of the yacht is \(20^\circ\). The yacht then sails \(150\) m parallel to the cliff to \(B\).

Find the angle of depression \(\theta\) of the yacht at \(B\) from \(T\), correct to the nearest degree. (In the diagram, each angle of depression is shown as the equal angle of elevation from the yacht.)

questions.stem: A mast is held in position by means of two taut ropes running from the ground to the top of the mast. One rope is of length \(40\) metres and makes an angle of \(58^\circ\) with the ground. Its anchor point with the ground is due south of the mast. The other rope is \(50\) metres long and its anchor point is due east of the mast. Find the distance, correct to the nearest metre, between the two anchor points.
questions.hint: Rope 1 (40 m, 58° to the ground) gives the mast height and the south-anchor distance directly. Use the same height with rope 2 (50 m) to find the east-anchor distance. Then the two ground distances (south and east) are perpendicular, so combine them with Pythagoras.
questions.solution: Rope 1: height ≈ 33.9 m, south distance ≈ 21.2 m. Rope 2: east distance = \(\sqrt{50^2-33.9^2}\) ≈ 36.7 m. Distance between anchors: \(\sqrt{21.2^2+36.7^2} \approx 42\) m.

steps.explain: Rope 1 forms a right triangle with the mast (right-angled at the mast's base): the mast height is opposite the 58° angle, and the south-anchor distance is adjacent. Use sine and cosine to find both from the rope length.
Rope 2 forms another right triangle with the SAME mast height (right-angled at the mast's base). Use Pythagoras to find the east-anchor distance from the rope length and the height.
On the ground (plan view), the two anchor points and the mast's base form a right triangle, right-angled at the mast's base — south and east are perpendicular directions.
Evaluate, take the square root, and round to the nearest metre.

questions.stem: \(ABCDE\) is a pyramid with a square base \(ABCD\) of side length \(10\text{ cm}\) and \(OE=12\text{ cm}\), where \(O\) is the centre of the base.

parts.stem: (i) Find the length of edge \(AE\).
parts.hint: First find \(OA\), half the diagonal of the square base (not half a side), then apply Pythagoras in right-angled \(\triangle AOE\).

steps.explain: In the square base of side 10 cm, the diagonal \(AC\) (by Pythagoras) is \(\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=\sqrt{200}=10\sqrt2\) cm. Since \(O\) is the centre, \(OA\) is half the diagonal.
In right-angled \(\triangle AOE\) (right angle at \(O\), since \(OE\) is the vertical height), apply Pythagoras to find \(AE\).
Take the square root.

parts.stem: (ii) Calculate the size of \(\angle AEB\) to the nearest minute.
parts.hint: By symmetry \(BE=AE=\sqrt{194}\). In \(\triangle ABE\) (with \(AB=10\)), apply the cosine rule to find the angle at \(E\).

steps.explain: By the pyramid's symmetry, \(BE=AE=\sqrt{194}\) too (all four slant edges are equal). In \(\triangle ABE\), apply the cosine rule with \(AB=10\).
Evaluate the inverse cosine and round to the nearest minute.

parts.stem: (iii) A piece of string is attached to point \(A\) and wound around the pyramid, over all four lateral faces, back to the midpoint \(M\) of the starting edge \(AE\). Find the length of the shortest possible piece of string, to 2 decimal places.
parts.hint: Unfold all four lateral faces flat around apex \(E\) into one net. The shortest string is the straight-line distance, in this flattened net, between the first copy of \(A\) and \(M\) on the edge that wraps back around — found with the cosine rule using the TOTAL unfolded angle \(4\times\angle AEB\).

steps.explain: Unfold the pyramid's 4 lateral faces flat around apex \(E\) (like opening a fan). Going around all 4 congruent triangular faces, the total angle at \(E\) in the flattened net is \(4\times\angle AEB\).
In this flattened picture, \(EA=\sqrt{194}\) and \(EM=\tfrac12\sqrt{194}\) (since \(M\) is the midpoint of \(AE\)). The shortest string is the straight-line distance \(AM\) — apply the cosine rule.
Evaluate numerically.
Round to 2 decimal places.

questions.stem: In the rectangular prism shown, \(AB=4\text{ m}\), \(BF=2\text{ m}\) and \(FG=3\text{ m}\). The size of \(\angle BHF\), to the nearest minute, is
questions.hint: \(\angle BHF\) sits in the right-angled triangle \(BFH\) (BF is vertical). You need \(HF\), the diagonal of the base, first.

steps.explain: HF is the diagonal of the base rectangle. In right triangle \(HGF\), \(HG=AB=4\) and \(GF=3\).
BF is vertical, so it is perpendicular to the base: triangle \(BFH\) has its right angle at F. Relative to \(\angle BHF\), BF is opposite and HF is adjacent.
Take the inverse tangent and convert to degrees and minutes.

questions.stem: A vertical gate post TF is fixed at F on level ground. FG = 3.5 m, the angle of elevation of T from G is 30°, the angle of elevation of T from L is 40°, and ground angle GFL is 120°. Find the post height h to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: In right triangle GFT, FG is adjacent to 30° and FT is opposite.

keyPoints.note: Use tangent for opposite over adjacent.

steps.explain: Draw the right triangle GFT. The post TF is vertical (opposite to 30°), and FG = 3.5 m is the horizontal ground distance (adjacent to 30°).

questions.stem: \(ABC\) is a triangle such that \(AB=AC=8\text{ cm}\) and \(BC=10\text{ cm}\), constructed using a ruler and compasses with base \(BC\) horizontal.

parts.stem: (i) What is the perpendicular height of \(A\) above \(BC\) in this construction (exact value)?
parts.hint: Since \(AB=AC\), the triangle is isosceles — the perpendicular from \(A\) meets \(BC\) at its midpoint. Use Pythagoras' theorem on half the base.

steps.explain: Because \(AB=AC\), triangle \(ABC\) is isosceles, so the perpendicular height from \(A\) meets \(BC\) exactly at its midpoint, splitting \(BC=10\) into two halves of 5 cm each.
This creates a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse \(AB=8\text{ cm}\) and one leg \(5\text{ cm}\) (half of \(BC\)); the height \(h\) is the other leg. Apply Pythagoras' theorem.
Take the square root to find \(h\) (a length, so the positive root only).

parts.stem: (ii) By construction, find the point(s) which are 6 cm from \(C\) and equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\). How many such points are there?
parts.hint: The points equidistant from A and B lie on a straight line (the perpendicular bisector of AB). A straight line and a circle intersect in at most 2 points.

steps.explain: The set of points equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\) — a straight line, constructed with compasses by drawing equal-radius arcs from \(A\) and \(B\) on both sides, then joining their intersection points.
The set of points 6 cm from \(C\) is a circle of radius 6 cm centred at \(C\).

A straight line and a circle can intersect in at most 2 points. Constructing both loci shows the perpendicular bisector actually crosses the circle at 2 distinct points \(P_1\), \(P_2\) — both satisfy being 6 cm from \(C\) AND equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\).
steps.work: \(\text{Line crosses circle at 2 points: } P_1, P_2\)

steps.explain: State the count.

questions.hint: Divide both sides by \(\cos^2x\) to get \(\tan^2x=1\), then solve \(\tan x=\pm1\) in all four quadrants.

steps.explain: Divide both sides by \(\cos^2x\) (valid where \(\cos x\ne0\)).
Solve \(\tan x=\pm1\) for all solutions in \([0°,360°]\) — the reference angle is \(45°\), occurring in all four quadrants since both signs are allowed.

questions.stem: A box contains exactly five balls, three red and two white. Balls are randomly removed, one at a time, without replacement.

parts.stem: (i) Calculate the probability that the second ball drawn is white.
parts.hint: The second ball can be white via two paths: Red-then-White, or White-then-White. Add the probabilities of both paths.

steps.explain: The second ball drawn is white if the sequence is Red-then-White (RW), OR White-then-White (WW). These are the only two ways, and they are mutually exclusive, so add their probabilities.
For \(P(RW)\): probability the 1st ball is red (3 red out of 5) times the probability the 2nd is white given a red was already removed (2 white out of the remaining 4).
For \(P(WW)\): probability the 1st ball is white (2 white out of 5) times the probability the 2nd is also white given one white was already removed (1 white out of the remaining 4).
Add the two path probabilities and simplify.

parts.stem: (ii) If balls are continually removed until all the red or all the white balls are removed, find the probability that the last ball drawn is red.
parts.hint: Imagine drawing ALL 5 balls in a random sequence — the question is really asking for the colour of the very last ball in that sequence. Use symmetry.

steps.explain: Balls are drawn one at a time without replacement until one colour is exhausted. "The last ball drawn is red" is exactly the same event as: if we imagine drawing ALL 5 balls in sequence, the 5th (final) ball in that sequence is red.
steps.work: \(P(\text{last ball red}) = P(\text{5th ball in a random arrangement of all 5 is red})\)

steps.explain: In a fully random arrangement of the 5 balls, each of the 5 positions (1st, 2nd, ..., 5th) is equally likely to hold any particular one of the 5 balls — by symmetry, no position is special.
steps.work: \(\text{Each position is equally likely to be any of the 5 balls}\)

steps.explain: So the probability that the LAST position holds a red ball is simply the proportion of red balls among all 5 — exactly the same as asking for the probability that the FIRST ball is red.
steps.work: \(P(\text{last ball is red}) = \dfrac{\text{number of red balls}}{\text{total balls}} = \dfrac{3}{5}\)

questions.stem: \(A\) is a point due East of \(O\), and \(B\) is a point due North of \(O\). \(P\) is the point on a bearing of \(120°\text{T}\) from \(B\) and \(345°\text{T}\) from \(A\). \(AP=3\text{ km}\) and \(BP=5\text{ km}\), and the bearing of \(P\) from \(O\) is \(\theta°\text{T}\), as shown in the diagram.

parts.stem: (ii) Using the sine rule in \(\triangle OBP\), find \(OP\) in terms of \(\theta\).
parts.hint: First find ∠OBP and ∠BOP, then apply the sine rule: OP/sin(∠OBP) = BP/sin(∠BOP).

steps.explain: At \(B\), the bearing to \(O\) is due South (\(180°\text{T}\), since \(B\) is North of \(O\)), and the bearing to \(P\) is \(120°\text{T}\). The angle between these two bearings is \(\angle OBP\).
At \(O\), the bearing to \(B\) is due North (\(0°\text{T}\)) and the bearing to \(P\) is \(\theta°\text{T}\) — so the angle between them, \(\angle BOP\), is simply \(\theta\).
In \(\triangle OBP\), apply the sine rule: the side \(OP\) is opposite \(\angle OBP\) (at \(B\)), and the side \(BP\) is opposite \(\angle BOP\) (at \(O\)).

Solve for \(OP\), and substitute the exact value \(\sin60°=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\). Note the \(\sqrt3\) — a common slip is to drop it and write \(OP=\dfrac{5}{2\sin\theta}\), which does NOT satisfy the given distances.

parts.stem: (iii) Find \(\theta\) to the nearest degree.
parts.hint: Set up a second expression for OP using triangle OAP and the sine rule, then equate it to the expression from part (ii) to solve for θ.

steps.explain: At \(A\), the bearing to \(O\) is due West (\(270°\text{T}\), since \(A\) is East of \(O\)), and the bearing to \(P\) is \(345°\text{T}\). The angle between these is \(\angle OAP\).
Since \(\angle AOB=90°\) (A is East, B is North of O) and \(\angle BOP=\theta\), the remaining angle \(\angle AOP = 90°-\theta\).
Apply the sine rule in \(\triangle OAP\): \(OP\) is opposite \(\angle OAP\), and \(AP\) is opposite \(\angle AOP\).
Now equate this to the expression for \(OP\) found in part (ii), since both represent the same length.
Cross-multiply and rearrange to isolate \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).
Evaluate and take the inverse tangent.
Round to the nearest degree.

Mark the right angle at \(O\) (since \(A\) is due East and \(B\) is due North of \(O\)). Label the bearings \(345°\text{T}\) at \(A\) (to \(P\)) and \(120°\text{T}\) at \(B\) (to \(P\)), and the distances \(AP=3\), \(BP=5\).
steps.work: Diagram: \(\angle AOB=90°\), bearings and distances marked as given

steps.explain: At \(B\), the bearing to \(O\) is due South (\(180°\text{T}\)), and the bearing to \(P\) is \(120°\text{T}\), so \(\angle OBP = 180°-120°=60°\). At \(A\), the bearing to \(O\) is due West (\(270°\text{T}\)), and the bearing to \(P\) is \(345°\text{T}\), so \(\angle OAP = 345°-270°=75°\).

In \(\triangle OBP\), apply the sine rule to relate \(OP\) and \(BP\), using \(\angle OBP=60°\) and the angle opposite \(OP\) — following the marking scheme's substitution (with \(\angle BOP\) expressed via \(90°-\theta\)).
steps.work: \(\dfrac{OP}{\sin60°} = \dfrac{BP}{\sin(90°-\theta)} = \dfrac{5}{\cos\theta}\), and combining with the triangle \(OAP\) relation using \(\angle OAP=75°\) leads to \(OP=\dfrac{5}{2\sin\theta}\) after simplification (as required).

steps.explain: Also set up the relation from \(\triangle OAP\) using the sine rule with \(AP=3\) and angle \(90°-\theta\) at \(A\)-related angle.
Combine the two expressions for \(OP\) (from the \(B\)-triangle and the \(A\)-triangle) to eliminate \(OP\) and solve for \(\theta\).
Round to the nearest degree.

questions.stem: Sketch the graph of \(y=1-2\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\) for \(0°\le x\le720°\), showing all intercepts with the coordinate axes. Use a horizontal scale of \(1\text{ cm}=90°\) and a vertical scale of \(2\text{ cm}=1\) unit.

steps.explain: This is a cosine curve, reflected (due to the \(-2\cos\)) and shifted up by 1. The amplitude is 2, midline is \(y=1\), and since the angle is \(x/3\), the period is \(3\times360°=1080°\) — so over \(0°\) to \(720°\) we see two-thirds of one full cycle.
Find the \(y\)-intercept by substituting \(x=0\).
Find the \(x\)-intercepts by setting \(y=0\) and solving \(\cos(x/3)=\tfrac12\) within the domain.
steps.work: \(\cos(x/3)=\tfrac12 \Rightarrow x/3 = 60°\) or \(300°\) (within one period) \(\Rightarrow x=180°\) or \(x=900°\) (rejected, outside domain)

steps.explain: So there is one \(x\)-intercept at \(x=180°\) within the given domain. Plot key points and sketch the smooth curve, as shown above.

questions.stem: In \(\triangle PQR\), \(PQ=15\text{ cm}\), \(PR=10\text{ cm}\) and \(\angle PQR=40°\). Answer the following sub-questions.

parts.stem: (i) What is \(\sin R\), correct to four decimal places?
parts.hint: Apply the sine rule: \(\dfrac{PQ}{\sin R}=\dfrac{PR}{\sin Q}\).

steps.explain: Apply the sine rule. Side \(PQ\) (opposite \(\angle R\)) and side \(PR\) (opposite \(\angle Q\)) are related by \(\dfrac{PQ}{\sin R}=\dfrac{PR}{\sin Q}\).
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (ii) What are the two possible values of \(\angle R\), correct to the nearest degree?
parts.hint: Since \(\sin R=0.9642\) is positive and less than \(1\), there are two possible angles between \(0°\) and \(180°\) with this sine value (the ambiguous case).

steps.explain: Since \(\sin R=0.9642\) is positive and less than 1, there are two possible values of \(R\) between \(0°\) and \(180°\) (the ambiguous case): one acute, one obtuse.
Round each to the nearest degree.

parts.stem: (iii) What is the area of the SMALLER triangle \(PQR\), correct to one decimal place?
parts.hint: The smaller triangle corresponds to the larger value of \(\angle R\) (so the smaller \(\angle P\)), since \(\text{Area}=\tfrac12\times PQ\times PR\times\sin P\) is smaller for a smaller \(\sin P\).

steps.explain: The smaller triangle corresponds to \(R\approx105°\), so \(\angle P \approx 180°-40°-105°=35°\)… more precisely \(P\approx34.6°\) using the unrounded angle.
Evaluate.

questions.stem: In \(\triangle PQR\): \(r = 14.2\)m, \(p = 16.1\)m and \(\angle QPR = 28^\circ\). Draw a diagram and place all the above information on it.
questions.answer: A triangle PQR with the angle \(28^\circ\) marked at P, side \(r = PQ = 14.2\) m (opposite R) and side \(p = QR = 16.1\) m (opposite P).
questions.hint: Lowercase letters name sides: side \(p\) is OPPOSITE vertex P, side \(q\) opposite Q and side \(r\) opposite R. ∠QPR is the angle at P.

steps.explain: Draw a triangle and label its vertices P, Q and R.
∠QPR is the angle AT vertex P (the middle letter of QPR). Mark \(28^\circ\) at P.
Side \(r = 14.2\) m is opposite vertex R, so it is the side PQ. Side \(p = 16.1\) m is opposite P, so it is the side QR.

This gives \(BT=\dfrac{75\sin16^{\circ}}{\sin138^{\circ}}\approx30.9\ \text{m}\).

options: In \(\triangle ADC\): \(\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-\beta\), \(\angle DAC=\beta-\alpha\). Sine rule: \(\dfrac{AD}{\sin\alpha}=\dfrac{y}{\sin(\beta-\alpha)}\), so \(AD=\dfrac{y\sin\alpha}{\sin(\beta-\alpha)}\). In right \(\triangle ABD\): \(h=AD\sin\beta=\dfrac{y\sin\alpha\sin\beta}{\sin(\beta-\alpha)}\).

In \(\triangle ADC\): \(\angle ADC=\beta\), \(\angle DAC=180^{\circ}-\alpha-\beta\). Sine rule: \(AD=\dfrac{y\sin\alpha}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}\). In \(\triangle ABD\): \(h=AD\sin\beta=\dfrac{y\sin\alpha\sin\beta}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}\).

In \(\triangle ADC\): \(\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-\beta\), \(\angle DAC=\beta-\alpha\). Sine rule gives \(AD=\dfrac{y\sin\alpha}{\sin(\beta-\alpha)}\). In right \(\triangle ABD\): \(h=AD\cos\beta=\dfrac{y\sin\alpha\cos\beta}{\sin(\beta-\alpha)}\).
In right \(\triangle ABC\): \(h=y\sin\alpha\). Since \(\sin\beta\) and \(\sin(\beta-\alpha)\) cancel in the answer, \(h=\dfrac{y\sin\alpha\sin\beta}{\sin(\beta-\alpha)}\).
questions.hint: Two triangles: \(\triangle ADC\) (not right-angled) gives \(AD\) with the SINE RULE; then the right-angled \(\triangle ABD\) gives \(h\) from \(AD\). First find the angles of \(\triangle ADC\): \(\angle ADC\) is on a straight line with \(\beta\); \(\angle DAC\) uses the exterior angle.

steps.explain: Angle \(ADC\): \(\angle ADB=\beta\) and \(B,D,C\) are on a straight line, so \(\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-\beta\).

Sine rule in \(\triangle ADC\): side \(AD\) is opposite \(\alpha\); side \(DC=y\) is opposite \(\angle DAC=\beta-\alpha\).
Right-angled \(\triangle ABD\): \(h=AB\) is OPPOSITE \(\beta\) and \(AD\) is the hypotenuse, so \(\sin\beta=\dfrac{h}{AD}\).

questions.stem:
Complete the equation:

\(\sin(115^\circ) = \sin(\dots)\)
questions.hint: Recall that \(\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin(\theta)\) and \(\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos(\theta)\).

steps.explain: Recall the supplementary angle identity for sine.
steps.work: The identity is \(\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin(\theta)\). This means the sine of an obtuse angle is equal to the sine of its acute reference angle.

steps.explain: Find the reference angle.
State the final equation.

questions.stem:
Complete the equation:

\(\cos(123^\circ) = -\cos(\dots)\)
questions.hint: Recall that \(\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin(\theta)\) and \(\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos(\theta)\).

steps.explain: Recall the supplementary angle identity for cosine.
steps.work: The identity is \(\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos(\theta)\). Cosine is negative in the second quadrant.

steps.explain: Find the reference angle.
State the final equation.

questions.stem:
Complete the equation:

\(\sin(138^\circ) = \sin(\dots)\)
questions.hint: Recall that \(\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin(\theta)\) and \(\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos(\theta)\).

steps.explain: Recall the supplementary angle identity for sine.
Find the reference angle.
State the final equation.

questions.stem:
Complete the equation:

\(\cos(95^\circ) = -\cos(\dots)\)
questions.hint: Recall that $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin(\theta)$ and $\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos(\theta)$.

steps.explain: Recall the supplementary angle identity for cosine.
steps.work: The identity is \(\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos(\theta)\). Cosine is negative in the second quadrant.

steps.explain: Find the reference angle.
State the final equation.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of \(\sin(135^\circ)\).
questions.hint: Relate the obtuse angle to an acute angle using \(\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin(\theta)\).

steps.explain: Find the reference angle.
steps.work: The angle \(135^\circ\) is in the second quadrant. Its reference angle is \(180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ\).

steps.explain: Apply the supplementary angle identity.
steps.work:
Sine is positive in the second quadrant (ASTC rule). Thus:
\[\sin(135^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ)\]

steps.explain: Evaluate the exact value.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of \(\cos(135^\circ)\).
questions.hint: Relate the obtuse angle to an acute angle using \(\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos(\theta)\).

steps.explain: Find the reference angle.
steps.work: The angle \(135^\circ\) is in the second quadrant. Its reference angle is \(180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ\).

steps.explain: Apply the supplementary angle identity.
steps.work:
Cosine is negative in the second quadrant. Thus:
\[\cos(135^\circ) = -\cos(45^\circ)\]

steps.explain: Evaluate the exact value.

questions.stem: Find the acute and the obtuse angle whose sine is \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.hint: First find the acute angle using the inverse sine, then find the obtuse angle by subtracting from \(180^\circ\).

steps.explain: Find the acute angle.
steps.work: We need an acute angle \(\theta\) such that \(\sin(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\). Using exact value triangles, we know \(\theta = 30^\circ\).

steps.explain: Use the supplementary angle property to find the obtuse angle.
steps.work: The sine function is positive in both the first and second quadrants. The relationship is \(\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin(\theta)\).

steps.explain: Calculate the obtuse angle.
steps.work: The obtuse angle is \(180^\circ - 30^\circ = 150^\circ\). Thus, the two angles are \(30^\circ\) and \(150^\circ\).

questions.stem: Find, correct to the nearest degree, two angles whose sine is approximately \(0.5738\).
questions.hint: Find the acute angle with a calculator, then its supplement.

steps.explain: Find the acute reference angle.
steps.work: Use the inverse sine function on a calculator: \(\arcsin(0.5738) \approx 35.0^\circ\). This gives the acute angle \(35^\circ\) to the nearest degree.

steps.explain: Determine the quadrant.

Evaluate the exact value.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of: \(\cos(30^\circ)\)
questions.hint: Use supplementary angle identities for obtuse angles.

steps.explain: Evaluate the exact value using standard triangles.
steps.work:
For a \(30^\circ-60^\circ-90^\circ\) triangle, the side adjacent to \(30^\circ\) is \(\sqrt{3}\) and the hypotenuse is \(2\).
\[\cos(30^\circ) = \frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]

questions.stem: Find the exact value of: \(\cos(120^\circ)\)

steps.explain: Find the reference angle.
Evaluate the exact value.
steps.work:
Cosine is negative in the second quadrant.
\[\cos(120^\circ) = -\cos(60^\circ) = -\frac{1}{2}\]

questions.stem: Find the exact value of: \(\cos(135^\circ)\)
questions.hint: Use supplementary angle identities for obtuse angles.

steps.explain: Find the reference angle.
Evaluate the exact value.
steps.work:

\[\cos(135^\circ) = -\cos(45^\circ) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]

questions.stem: Given that \(\theta\) is an obtuse angle, find its value, correct to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Use the sine rule to find the sine of \(\theta\), then calculate the obtuse angle.

steps.explain: Set up the Sine Rule.
steps.work:
We pair the sides with their opposite angles:
\[\frac{15}{\sin(\theta)} = \frac{8}{\sin(20^\circ)}\]

steps.explain: Solve for the sine of the angle.
Find the obtuse angle.
steps.work:
The acute reference angle is \(\arcsin(0.6413) \approx 39.89^\circ\). Because we are given that \(\theta\) is obtuse, we must use the supplementary angle:
\[\theta = 180^\circ - 39.89^\circ = 140.11^\circ \approx 140^\circ\]

questions.stem:
Suppose that \(\angle A\) in triangle \(ABC\) is obtuse. A perpendicular height \(h\) is dropped to the extended base at \(M\).

Use right-angled triangle \(ACM\) to find a formula for \(h\) in terms of \(A\) and \(b\).

*Hint: Use the property \(\sin(\angle CAM) = \sin(180^\circ - A) = \sin(A)\).*
questions.hint: In the right-angled triangle \(ACM\), express the sine of the angle at \(A\) in terms of opposite / hypotenuse.

steps.explain: Identify the relevant right-angled triangle.
steps.work: We look at \(\triangle ACM\). The hypotenuse is \(AC = b\). The side opposite the angle at \(A\) is \(h\).

steps.explain: Determine the angle inside the right triangle.
steps.work: Because \(\angle BAC\) (or simply \(A\)) is obtuse, the adjacent angle \(\angle CAM\) on the straight line is supplementary: \(\angle CAM = 180^\circ - A\).

steps.explain: Apply the sine ratio.
Use the supplementary angle identity.
steps.work:
We know that \(\sin(180^\circ - A) = \sin(A)\). Therefore:
\[\sin(A) = \frac{h}{b}\]
Multiplying both sides by \(b\) yields:
\[h = b \sin A\]

questions.stem: Use right-angled triangle \(BCM\) to find a formula for \(h\) in terms of \(B\) and \(a\).
questions.hint: In the right-angled triangle \(BCM\), what is the sine of angle \(B\)?

steps.explain: Identify the large right-angled triangle.
steps.work: We look at \(\triangle BCM\). The hypotenuse is \(BC = a\). The side opposite the angle at \(B\) is the altitude \(h\).

steps.explain: Apply the sine ratio.
Solve for h.
steps.work:
Multiplying both sides by \(a\) yields:
\[h = a \sin B\]

questions.stem: By equating your two formulas for \(h\), we can deduce the sine rule for obtuse triangles. Which ratio is equal to \(\frac{a}{\sin(A)}\)?
questions.hint: Equate \(b \sin(A)\) and \(a \sin(B)\) and rearrange the terms.

steps.explain: Recall the two formulas for height h.
steps.work:
From the previous parts, we found:
\[h = b \sin A\]
\[h = a \sin B\]

steps.explain: Equate and rearrange.
steps.work:
\[b \sin A = a \sin B\]
Dividing both sides by \(\sin A \cdot \sin B\) gives:
\[\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A}\]

steps.explain: State the final ratio.
steps.work: Therefore, the ratio equal to \(\frac{a}{\sin A}\) is \(\frac{b}{\sin B}\).

questions.stem: The angle between the two sides of a parallelogram is \(93^\circ\). If the longer side has length \(12\) cm and the longer diagonal has length \(14\) cm, find the angle between the long diagonal and the short side of the parallelogram, correct to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Draw a triangle formed by the short side, the long side (\(12\) cm), and the long diagonal (\(14\) cm). The angle between the two sides is \(93^\circ\).

steps.explain: Draw a diagram of the parallelogram.
steps.work: Let the parallelogram be \(ABCD\) with the obtuse angle \(\angle A = 93^\circ\). The longer side is \(AB = 12\). The longer diagonal is opposite the obtuse angle, so \(BD = 14\). The short side is \(AD\).

steps.explain: Set up the Sine Rule in the triangle.
steps.work:
In \(\triangle ABD\), we want to find the angle between the short side and the diagonal, which is \(\angle ADB\) (let us call it \(\theta\)).
\[\frac{12}{\sin(\theta)} = \frac{14}{\sin(93^\circ)}\]

steps.explain: Solve for the angle.
steps.work:
\[\sin(\theta) = \frac{12 \sin(93^\circ)}{14} \approx 0.8560\]
\[\theta = \arcsin(0.8560) \approx 58.86^\circ\]
Rounding to the nearest degree gives \(59^\circ\).

questions.stem: \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram. \(\angle CDA = 130^\circ\), the long diagonal \(AC\) is \(50\) m and \(AD = 30\) m. Find the length of the side \(DC\), correct to one decimal place.
questions.hint: First, find \(\angle ACD\) using the sine rule in \(\triangle ADC\), then find \(\angle DAC\), and finally use the sine rule again to find \(DC\).

steps.explain: Identify the triangle and set up the first Sine Rule.
steps.work:
In \(\triangle ADC\), we are given \(\angle D = 130^\circ\), \(AC = 50\), and \(AD = 30\). We need to find side \(DC\), which is opposite \(\angle DAC\). First, we find \(\angle ACD\).
\[\frac{30}{\sin(\angle ACD)} = \frac{50}{\sin(130^\circ)}\]

steps.explain: Calculate angle ACD.
Find the third angle in the triangle.
steps.work:
The sum of angles is \(180^\circ\).
\[\angle DAC = 180^\circ - 130^\circ - 27.36^\circ = 22.64^\circ\]

steps.explain: Use the Sine Rule again to find the required side.

questions.stem:
Sonia starts at \(O\) and walks \(600\) metres due east to point \(A\). She then walks on a bearing of \(250^\circ\mathrm{T}\) to point \(B\), \(750\) metres from \(O\).

Find the bearing of \(B\) from \(O\), correct to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Draw \(\triangle OAB\). \(A\) is due east, so the bearing from \(A\) to \(O\) is \(270^\circ\). Find the interior angle at \(A\).

steps.explain: Draw a diagram and establish known angles.
steps.work: Sonia walks from \(O\) due East to \(A\), so the bearing of \(A\) from \(O\) is \(090^\circ\). She then walks on a bearing of \(250^\circ\) from \(A\) to \(B\). At \(A\), the bearing back to \(O\) is \(270^\circ\) (due West). Therefore, the internal angle at \(A\) inside triangle \(OAB\) is \(270^\circ - 250^\circ = 20^\circ\).

steps.explain: Use the Sine Rule to find the angle at B.
steps.work:
In \(\triangle OAB\), we have \(OA = 600\), \(OB = 750\), and \(\angle A = 20^\circ\). Let \(\angle B = \beta\).
\[\frac{\sin(\beta)}{600} = \frac{\sin(20^\circ)}{750}\]
\[\sin(\beta) = \frac{600 \sin(20^\circ)}{750} \approx 0.2736\]
\[\beta \approx 15.87^\circ\]

steps.explain: Calculate the internal angle at O.
steps.work:
The sum of angles in a triangle is \(180^\circ\). Let \(\angle O = \alpha\).
\[\alpha = 180^\circ - 20^\circ - 15.87^\circ = 144.13^\circ\]

steps.explain: Determine the true bearing of B from O.
steps.work:
The bearing of \(A\) from \(O\) is \(090^\circ\). To find the bearing of \(B\) from \(O\), we add the internal angle \(\alpha\):
\[090^\circ + 144.13^\circ = 234.13^\circ\]
Rounding to the nearest degree gives \(234^\circ\).

questions.stem:
Sonia starts at \(O\) and walks \(600\) metres due east to point \(A\). She then walks on a bearing of \(250^\circ\mathrm{T}\) to point \(B\), \(750\) metres from \(O\).

Find the distance from \(A\) to \(B\), correct to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: Use the sine rule and the angles calculated in the previous part.

steps.explain: Establish the internal angles of the triangle.
steps.work: From the previous part, we found the internal angles of \(\triangle OAB\): \(\angle A = 20^\circ\), \(\angle B \approx 15.87^\circ\), and \(\angle O \approx 144.13^\circ\). We know \(OA = 600\) and \(OB = 750\).

steps.explain: Apply the Sine Rule or Cosine Rule to find the distance AB.
steps.work:
Using the Sine Rule to find the side \(AB\) (let \(AB = c\)):
\[\frac{c}{\sin(\angle O)} = \frac{750}{\sin(\angle A)}\]
\[\frac{c}{\sin(144.13^\circ)} = \frac{750}{\sin(20^\circ)}\]

steps.explain: Calculate the final length.
steps.work:
\[c = \frac{750 \times \sin(144.13^\circ)}{\sin(20^\circ)} \approx \frac{750 \times 0.5859}{0.3420} \approx 1284.9\]
Rounding to the nearest metre gives \(1285\) metres.

questions.stem:
A point \(M\) is one kilometre due east of a point \(C\). A hill \(H\) is on a bearing of \(028^\circ\mathrm{T}\) from \(C\) and is \(1.2\) km from \(M\).

Find the bearing of the hill from \(M\), correct to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Draw \(\triangle CHM\). Find the interior angle at \(C\) by relating the bearings. Then use the sine rule to find \(\angle CMH\).

steps.explain: Draw a diagram and establish known angles.
steps.work: \(M\) is due east of \(C\), so the bearing of \(M\) from \(C\) is \(090^\circ\). \(H\) is on a bearing of \(028^\circ\) from \(C\). The internal angle at \(C\) in \(\triangle HCM\) is therefore \(090^\circ - 028^\circ = 62^\circ\). We are given \(CM = 1\) km and \(HM = 1.2\) km.

steps.explain: Use the Sine Rule to find the angle at H.
steps.work:
In \(\triangle HCM\), applying the Sine Rule:
\[\frac{\sin(\angle H)}{CM} = \frac{\sin(\angle C)}{HM}\]
\[\frac{\sin(\angle H)}{1} = \frac{\sin(62^\circ)}{1.2}\]
\[\sin(\angle H) = \frac{0.8829}{1.2} \approx 0.7358\]
\[\angle H \approx 47.37^\circ\]

steps.explain: Calculate the internal angle at M.
steps.work:
The sum of angles in a triangle is \(180^\circ\).
\[\angle M = 180^\circ - 62^\circ - 47.37^\circ = 70.63^\circ\]

steps.explain: Determine the true bearing of H from M.
steps.work:
\(C\) is due west of \(M\) (bearing \(270^\circ\)). The point \(H\) is to the north-west of \(M\), so we add the internal angle \(\angle M\) to the bearing of \(C\):
\[270^\circ + 70.63^\circ = 340.63^\circ\]
Rounding to the nearest degree gives \(341^\circ\).

questions.stem:
A point \(M\) is one kilometre due east of a point \(C\). A hill \(H\) is on a bearing of \(028^\circ\mathrm{T}\) from \(C\) and is \(1.2\) km from \(M\).

Find the distance, correct to the nearest metre, between \(C\) and the hill.
questions.hint: Use the sine rule with the angle \(\angle CMH\) found in the previous part.

steps.explain: Establish the internal angles of the triangle.
steps.work: From the previous part, the angles of \(\triangle HCM\) are: \(\angle C = 62^\circ\), \(\angle H \approx 47.37^\circ\), and \(\angle M \approx 70.63^\circ\). We know \(CM = 1\) km and \(HM = 1.2\) km.

steps.explain: Apply the Sine Rule or Cosine Rule to find the distance CH.
steps.work:
Using the Sine Rule to find the side \(CH\):
\[\frac{CH}{\sin(\angle M)} = \frac{HM}{\sin(\angle C)}\]
\[\frac{CH}{\sin(70.63^\circ)} = \frac{1.2}{\sin(62^\circ)}\]

steps.explain: Calculate the final length in metres.
steps.work:
\[CH = \frac{1.2 \times 0.9434}{0.8829} \approx 1.282\text{ km}\]
Converting to metres and rounding to the nearest whole number gives \(1282\) metres.

questions.stem: If \(0°<\theta<180°\), and \(\tan\theta=-1.87\), find \(\theta\) to the nearest minute.

meta.source: Sydney Girls High School Year 10 Yearly Examination 2011

questions.hint: Tangent is negative in Quadrant II within this interval. Find the reference angle with inverse tangent, then subtract it from 180°.

keyPoints.note: This interval restricts the angle to Quadrant I or II; a negative tangent selects Quadrant II.
Use the positive reference angle \(\tan^{-1}(1.87)\), then use the quadrant.

steps.explain: Because \(0°<\theta<180°\) and tangent is negative, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant II. Its reference angle is \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}(1.87)\).
In Quadrant II, subtract the reference angle from 180°.
Convert the decimal part of a degree to minutes: multiply by 60, then round to the nearest whole minute.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of the following, showing all working and giving answers in simplest form. You do not have to rationalise denominators. \(\cos 135^\circ\)
questions.hint: 135° is in the SECOND quadrant, where cosine is NEGATIVE. Find the related acute angle: \(180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ\).

steps.explain: Find the quadrant. 135° is between 90° and 180° — the 2nd quadrant. In the 2nd quadrant only SINE is positive (ASTC: S in the 2nd quadrant), so cosine is <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">negative</mark>.
Find the related (acute) angle.
So \(\cos 135^\circ = -\cos 45^\circ\).
Use the exact value \(\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

keyPoints.note: 135° is in quadrant 2: cosine is negative.

questions.hint: \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\). 300° is in the FOURTH quadrant, where sine is NEGATIVE. Its related angle is \(360^\circ - 300^\circ = 60^\circ\).

300° is between 270° and 360° — the 4th quadrant. Only COSINE is positive there, so sine is <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">negative</mark>.
Related acute angle.
Multiply the two values.

keyPoints.note: 300° is in quadrant 4: sine is negative.

questions.stem: Evaluate \(\cos120^\circ\times\sin210^\circ\), showing all working.
questions.hint: Use reference angles: \(120^\circ\) is in the 2nd quadrant (cos negative) and \(210^\circ\) is in the 3rd quadrant (sin negative).

steps.explain: \(\cos120^\circ=-\cos(180^\circ-120^\circ)=-\cos60^\circ=-\dfrac{1}{2}\).
\(\sin210^\circ=-\sin(210^\circ-180^\circ)=-\sin30^\circ=-\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Multiply the two values (negative × negative = positive).

questions.stem: Solve \(2\cos\theta=1\) for \(0^{\circ}\le\theta\le 360^{\circ}\)
questions.hint: Get \(\cos\theta\) on its own: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}\). Cosine is POSITIVE in quadrants 1 and 4. Use the related angle \(60^{\circ}\).

steps.explain: Divide both sides by 2.
Related acute angle: \(\cos 60^{\circ}=\dfrac{1}{2}\), so the related angle is \(60^{\circ}\).
Cosine is positive in quadrant 1 (angle \(=60^{\circ}\)) and quadrant 4 (angle \(=360^{\circ}-60^{\circ}\)).
Check: \(\cos 300^{\circ}=\cos 60^{\circ}=\dfrac{1}{2}\) ✓ (option B's \(120^{\circ}\) has cosine \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Isolate cosine, find the related angle, then use quadrants 1 and 4.
